title: Air passenger duty
headline: £8 to £106 on an economy ticket. Each £1 more raises about £0.13bn.
description: Add to the duty on every economy-class ticket departing a UK airport, in pounds on top of the rates already planned. The reduced rate is £8 for a domestic flight and £15, £102 or £106 by distance band from April 2026, rising with inflation in April 2027.

baselinePolicy.text: Reduced (economy) rates from 1 April 2026: domestic £8, band A £15, band B £102, band C £106; from 1 April 2027: £8.26, £15.49, £105.33 and £109.46. Autumn Budget 2024 raised all rates from 2026-27 and the private-jet rate by a further 50%; Budget 2025 extends the higher rate to all private jets over 5.7 tonnes from April 2027 (Table 4.1 line 58).
alreadyIncludes: All rates raised from April 2026, with the higher rate on larger private jets up 50% (Autumn Budget 2024, Table 5.1 line 34).
Higher rate extended to all private jets over 5.7 tonnes from 1 April 2027 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 58).

control.formatLabel: on every economy ticket, on top of the planned rates

uprating.head: receiptsByTax.airPassengerDuty
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR's air passenger duty receipts forecast (Table A.5) (ADR-0004).

caveats: HMRC publishes the effect of £1 on the reduced rate; larger changes are scaled linearly here. HMRC publishes an increase only, so the slider only rises. The £1 is added to every reduced-rate band alike; the standard and higher rates (premium cabins and private jets) are not moved by this lever.

HMRC's estimates are on its Spring Statement 2025 indexed baseline for an April 2026 start. This tool shifts the profile to the chosen start year and scales it by the growth of the relevant OBR receipts head in the March 2026 forecast; the underlying level is not rebased. HMRC deferred its 2026 edition to review key assumptions.

considerations.text: HMRC's figure is a direct effect on this tax and closely related tax bases. It includes HMRC's standard behavioural response, but not wider effects on the economy, which HMRC says are usually captured in the OBR's economy forecast instead.

The duty is paid per passenger by the airline and passed on in fares, so it falls on people who fly, more of whom are better off; a flat pound on the economy rate is the same on a £30 domestic hop as on a long-haul ticket, and domestic return flights pay it twice.

HMRC postponed the 2026 edition of these estimates (due 7 July 2026) to complete a review of the key assumptions behind some of them, after the Office for Statistics Regulation asked for more transparency about pre- and post-behavioural estimates. The figures here are HMRC's June 2025 estimates.
